newsitem.title: PERU: Peru Congress ousts constitutional court judges.
newsitem.headline: Peru Congress ousts constitutional court judges.

text.p: Peru's Congress voted Thursday to remove three Constitutional Court judges who rejected a law that would have cleared the way for a third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori.

The fate of a fourth judge and president of the court, Ricardo Nugent, was left undecided as the government-controlled Congress decided to further analyse his role in the autonomous body's rulings on the the reelection law.

After a debate of almost 15 hours, opposition legislators held up hand-painted banners reading, "Defend democracy" and "No to the smashing of the Constitutional Court". But just after midnight, the motion to remove the judges was passed with 52 votes in favour, 33 against and one abstention.

"This result is nothing but a political manoeuvre -- a mockery," opposition congressman Alva Orlandini said. "In effect the Congressional majority has managed to sack (the judges) for acting according to independent criteria and carrying out their autonomous functions."
The government ousted the judges, accusing them of acting improperly when they passed judgment on the reelection law after three members of the court refused to issue a legal interpretation.

"The accusation strengthens democratic stability," said government supporter Enrique Chirinos, who was a member of a congressional commission that investigated the judges. "With the court functioning like this and making Peru ungovernable, you have to make the institutions respect the constitution of the state."
Valentin Paniagua, a lawyer for the judges, told Congress: "These people have not committed any wrong and, in fact, the interests of those who want to keep Fujimori in power are really behind this,"

Local polls taken before Thursday's vote showed the moves against the judges were hurting Fujimori's popularity ratings as most Peruvians believed the government was abusing its power and trying to take revenge on the judges for their decision.
Peruvian law is ambiguous on whether Fujimori, who became president in 1990 and was reelected after rewriting the constitution in 1995, can run for an unprecedented third term in 2000.

The accused judges issued two separate rulings on a government-sponsored law designed to allow Fujimori to run again. The interpretiations over the decision meant the president was left with an insecure legal platform from which to launch his candidacy.
While government legislators said the court ratified their favourable interpretation, the opposition claimed a third election bid would be illegal.
